means:
Able to be **defended, held, or maintained** — of a position, theory, claim, or job.

It began as a military word (a fort you can hold against attack) and now lives mostly in argument: a tenable theory is one that survives cross-examination. Note how modest it is — tenable doesn't mean *true* or *convincing*, only that it hasn't yet been demolished. "Her reading of the poem is tenable" is a long way from praise; it means you can't quite disprove it. Applied to a job or a situation, it shifts to *survivable*: a position that can still be occupied without collapse.
trap:
⚠️ **tenable ≠ tenuous.**
- **tenable** = holds up
- **tenuous** = thin, flimsy, barely holding on

They look like cousins and are near-opposites: a tenuous argument is exactly the one that isn't tenable.
trick_line: You'll almost always meet it wearing the **un-**: *his position became untenable, so he resigned.*
trick_unpack: Define it backwards from the far commoner *untenable* — whatever can't be held is untenable, so tenable is the fort still standing.
sentences: No **tenable** account of the manuscript's provenance has yet been offered, though three have been attempted.
Blaming the intern for a decision he made himself wasn't a **tenable** line and he knew it.
in_the_wild: Political journalism runs on the negative: when a minister's "position becomes **untenable**", that's the standard press signal that a resignation lands within the week.
etymology: Latin **tenēre** = *"to hold"* — one of the great GRE root-mines: **tenacious** (holding on), **tenant** (one who holds property), **tenure** (the holding of a post), **tenet** (a belief you hold), plus **retain, contain, sustain, detain, abstain**.
one_line: Able to be defended or maintained under attack.
